final_proof:
Let
\[
a_n=\Pr(X=n),\qquad b_n=\Pr(Y=n)\quad(n\geq 0).
\]
If a natural-number convention omits \(0\), simply take \(a_0=b_0=0\). Since \(X\) and \(Y\) take values in the natural numbers, their probability generating functions are
\[
\Pi_X(s)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_ns^n,\qquad
\Pi_Y(s)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}b_ns^n.
\]
For every \(s\in[-1,1]\), these series converge absolutely, because
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|a_ns^n|\leq \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n=1,
\]
and likewise for \(Y\).

First suppose that \(\Pr(X=n)=\Pr(Y=n)\) for every natural number \(n\). Thus \(a_n=b_n\) for every \(n\geq0\), including the harmless zero terms corresponding to values outside either random variable's codomain. The two absolutely convergent series above then agree term by term, so \(\Pi_X(s)=\Pi_Y(s)\) for every \(s\in[-1,1]\).

Conversely, suppose that
\[
\Pi_X(s)=\Pi_Y(s)\qquad\text{for every }s\in[-1,1].
\]
We prove by induction on \(k\geq0\) that \(a_k=b_k\). At \(s=0\), equality of the generating functions gives \(a_0=b_0\).

Now fix \(k\geq1\) and suppose \(a_j=b_j\) for all \(j<k\). For every \(s\in(0,1)\), equality of the generating functions and cancellation of their first \(k\) terms give
\[
0=\sum_{n=k}^{\infty}(a_n-b_n)s^n.
\]
Dividing by \(s^k\), we obtain
\[
0=a_k-b_k+R_k(s),
\qquad
R_k(s):=\sum_{n=k+1}^{\infty}(a_n-b_n)s^{n-k}.
\]
The remainder satisfies
\[
|R_k(s)|
\leq \sum_{n=k+1}^{\infty}(a_n+b_n)s^{n-k}
\leq s\sum_{n=k+1}^{\infty}(a_n+b_n)
\leq 2s.
\]
Hence \(R_k(s)\to0\) as \(s\downarrow0\). Taking that limit in the displayed identity yields \(a_k-b_k=0\). This completes the induction and proves
\[
\Pr(X=k)=\Pr(Y=k)\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb N.
\]
Thus the two probability generating functions agree on \([-1,1]\) if and only if the two probability mass functions agree at every natural number.
